A film about what happens when a public decision is treated as the end of the story.

Independent fictional development concept
Michael Needs / Gizmet
A working concept. The town, decision and participants below are fictional. Images are generated illustrations. This is a proposed film, with no secured access, commission or contributor agreement.

Case file ● 001

01 / The questionProposed feature documentary

A town is told its public archive will close. The decision is final. The record behind it is less clear.

Who signed it off?

We follow the people who will live with the closure as they try to understand how it was decided. Meeting minutes, correspondence and the accounts of those in the room become a map of the process.

The central question is simple: who shaped a decision presented as inevitable, and what alternatives were considered? The stakes are the town’s access to its own history and its faith in public decisions.

02 / The worldWhere the decision lands
01–02

We begin with a researcher trying to consult a file, a family tracing a name and a local historian confronting a locked door. Their needs give the decision human scale before the film turns to the paperwork.

We return to ordinary places between each discovery. The building, the street, the people who use it: a public decision is also a change to daily life.

03 / The filmOne feature · Three movements

The answer is in the sequence.

Act I / Consequence

The closed door

We meet the people affected and establish what is at risk. Their questions set the investigation in motion. The film observes the gap between an official notice and the lives it reaches.

Act II / Decision

Follow the paper

We reconstruct the chronology through records and interviews. Each document is dated, placed in context and tested against another account. The film distinguishes what was said, what was recorded and what remains unknown.

Act III / Reply

The room reopens

We put the emerging account to the decision makers and invite their response. The ending rests on what the record can support, while leaving genuine uncertainty visible. The community’s next steps provide the final movement.

04 / The recordMethod on screen

Every claim has a route back.

Documents are filmed as physical objects, then translated into clean on-screen timelines. The audience can see where a statement came from, when it was made and which part of the story it supports. We use source labels and dates in the finished film; this concept page contains no purported case evidence.

05 / The imageVisual treatment

Observe the place.
Read the trace.

A close, patient camera stays with people and spaces. Records are filmed in close detail so viewers can read the evidence. Red thread marks the movement between a source, a decision and its consequences.

View original treatment spread ↗

Camera. Observational portraits, empty civic spaces and small physical details. Faces belong to contributors only when access is agreed.

Graphics. One typographic system for chronology, source and uncertainty. Motion follows a line of inquiry, then stops so the viewer can read.

Sound. Room tone, paper and place carry transitions. Silence holds when an answer is missing.

06 / The propositionIndependent concept

An apparently settled story becomes less certain, one document at a time.

This treatment demonstrates how an investigative film can be pitched as an experience: legible at a glance, substantial on a second reading and coherent on paper. It is an independent fictional development study by Michael Needs.
